claims.text: Wear resistance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by grain-boundary segregation.
Segregation-stabilized nanoscale microstructures impede plastic deformation during wear.
Changing processing so as to enhance or disrupt grain-boundary segregation will systematically alter wear performance.
A typical as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating has a largely random elemental distribution with emergent but unoptimized grain-boundary segregation.
A typical as-deposited high-entropy-alloy coating contains nanoscale phase distributions.
Annealing temperature or duration can be selected to accentuate or diminish grain-boundary segregation relative to baseline processing.
Enhanced grain-boundary segregation stabilizes nanocrystalline phases.
Stabilization of nanocrystalline phases increases coating hardness.
Stabilization of nanocrystalline phases reduces dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility mitigates wear by reducing plastic deformation during surface interaction.
Coatings with thermally enhanced grain-boundary segregation will have a lower wear rate than the baseline.
Coatings with thermally enhanced grain-boundary segregation will have higher hardness than the baseline.
Treatments that reduce grain-boundary segregation will increase wear rates.
Untreated baseline coatings possess an uncontrolled level of grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale phase distribution.
The proposed segregation effect should be observable in high-entropy-alloy coatings produced under similar deposition conditions.
The relative contribution of grain-boundary segregation may vary among alloy systems and may be confounded by residual stress or precipitate formation.
